content: For patients with genotype 2 infection or an unknown/mixed genotype population, the percentage of patients achieving sustained virologic response at 12 weeks (SVR12) ranged from 86% to 90%. The quality of evidence, as assessed by the GRADE system, was rated as moderate in both analyses. In patients with cirrhosis treated with sofosbuvir, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir, evidence was available for those with genotypes 1 and 3, as well as for populations with unknown or mixed genotypes. The SVR12 rates ranged from 95% to 96%, with GRADE assessments varying from very low to high across outcomes. For treatment-naïve patients with cirrhosis treated with sofosbuvir, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir, evidence was limited to those with genotype 3 infection. No observational studies were identified, and the GRADE assessment was moderate. For treatment-experienced patients with cirrhosis treated with sofosbuvir, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir, evidence was available for genotypes 1 and 3, as well as for unknown or mixed genotypes. The SVR12 rates ranged from 95% to 96%, with GRADE assessments ranging from very low to high. For patients with cirrhosis and genotype 3 infection treated with daclatasvir, sofosbuvir, and ribavirin, the pooled SVR12 rates ranged from 86% to 91%, with GRADE assessed as low. No evidence was identified for genotype 2 infection. In treatment-naïve patients with cirrhosis treated with daclatasvir, sofosbuvir, and ribavirin, evidence was available only for genotype 3 infection. The SVR12 rates ranged from 83% to 98%, with GRADE assessed as very low. In treatment-experienced patients with cirrhosis treated with daclatasvir, sofosbuvir, and ribavirin, evidence was limited to genotype 3 infection. A single clinical trial (N=30) reported an SVR12 rate of 87%, with GRADE assessed as low. No observational studies were identified. For patients with cirrhosis and genotypes 2 or 3 infection treated with sofosbuvir and ribavirin, the pooled SVR12 rates ranged from 61% to 86%, with GRADE assessed as low in all cases. In treatment-naïve patients with cirrhosis treated with sofosbuvir and ribavirin, evidence was available for genotypes 2 and 3, with pooled SVR12 rates ranging from 61% to 85%. GRADE was assessed as low. In treatment-experienced patients with cirrhosis treated with sofosbuvir and ribavirin, evidence was available for genotypes 2 and 3. The pooled SVR12 rates ranged from 57% to 82%, with GRADE assessments varying from low to moderate. For patients with HIV co-infection, pooled SVR12 rates were reported by genotype in an all-treatment experience population. The SVR12 rates were generally high, though the number of studies and sample sizes were limited. For patients with HIV co-infection treated with daclatasvir and sofosbuvir, evidence was available only for mixed or unknown genotypes across two observational studies (N=347). The pooled SVR12 rate was 87%, with GRADE assessed as very low. For patients with HIV co-infection treated with elbasvir and grazoprevir, evidence was available for genotypes 1, 4, and 6, as well as for unknown or mixed genotypes. The SVR12 rates ranged from 83% to 96%, with GRADE assessments varying from very low to moderate. For patients with HIV co-infection treated with glecaprevir and pibrentasvir, evidence was available only for an unknown or mixed genotype population from a single observational study. The SVR12 rate was 100%, with GRADE assessed as high. For patients with HIV co-infection treated with ledipasvir and sofosbuvir, evidence was available for genotypes 1 and 4, as well as for unknown or mixed genotypes. The SVR12 rates ranged from 75% to 98%, with GRADE assessments varying from very low to high. For patients with HIV co-infection treated with paritaprevir/ritonavir, ombitasvir, and dasabuvir, evidence was available only for genotype 1 infection in an observational study. The SVR12 rate was 86%, with GRADE assessed as very low due to the small sample size (N=7). For patients with HIV co-infection treated with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir, evidence was available for genotypes 1–4. The SVR12 rates ranged from 92% to 96%, with GRADE assessments varying from very low to low. Safety outcomes, including discontinuations due to adverse events (DAEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), and mortality, were reported for all treatments except daclatasvir, sofosbuvir, and ribavirin. The incidence of SAEs was very low across treatments, ranging from 1% to 5%, with GRADE assessments varying from moderate to high. Mortality rates were also very low, ranging from 0% to 4%, with GRADE assessments rated as high for all treatments. In summary, most treatments achieved high SVR12 rates, with GRADE assessments often rated as high or moderate. However, evidence for genotypes 2 and 3, particularly in patients with cirrhosis, was mixed and often limited by small sample sizes. For patients with HIV co-infection, SVR12 rates were generally high, though evidence was limited. Safety outcomes were favorable, with low rates of SAEs and mortality across treatments.
